messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Photographer
  trauma_type: Combat
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Belong Nowhere: I no longer belong anywhere, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Minh was 18 when he first came into treatment, a single South Eastern Asian American photographer who had spent the past year trying to make sense of how quickly his life had changed after combat. He described the deployment in a way that was careful but vivid, as though he still saw it with a clarity that did not fade. One moment that stayed with him involved an attack during a routine stretch of duty, when what had seemed like an ordinary part of the day turned dangerous without warning. He remembered the sounds first, then the confusion of movement, and then the awful awareness that other people around him were in immediate danger. In the aftermath, one image returned to him with particular force: the sense that he should have done more, moved faster, protected others better. He had come to replay that moment not as a distant memory but as something that still felt close enough to touch, and he spoke about it with a tight jaw and a visible strain, as if he were trying to keep control of the picture in his mind.

Over time, Minh noticed that memories of the event did not come to him like ordinary recollections. They arrived with an unnerving sharpness, more real and vivid than the memories of everyday things, as if his mind were dropping him back into the scene without warning. He described how a smell, a sudden metallic noise, or the sight of a crowded street could instantly bring back the full memory before he had a chance to brace himself. In those moments, he felt the same surge of rage he had felt after the attack, directed at the chaos of it, at the people who had been hurt, and at himself for not preventing more damage. He said the feeling could be so intense that it left him angry for hours, though he did not usually show it openly. He kept his expression controlled, but he also seemed embarrassed by how fast the memories could overtake him, especially when he was in places where he could not easily leave.

Minh’s sense of safety had changed in practical ways as well. He said he was no longer able to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place, including his own apartment, where he would still sit facing the door or check the windows before settling down. Ordinary sounds made him jump in ways that startled other people: a slammed car door outside, a sharp notification from his phone, or someone calling his name unexpectedly could make him flinch before he could stop himself. He noticed that he had begun taking too many risks and doing things that could cause him harm, almost as if he no longer handled his own well-being with the same caution he used to have. He did not describe this as wanting to die, but rather as a kind of reckless disregard for himself that had emerged after the combat and that he found difficult to explain. He sounded unsettled by his own behavior, as though he recognized it did not fit the person he had been before.

As the months passed, Minh’s thoughts about himself and other people became harsher and more fixed. He had come to believe that he no longer belonged anywhere, not fully in the military world he had left behind and not comfortably in civilian life either. At home, among family and familiar community spaces, he felt separated by experiences he could not easily translate into conversation. With people his own age, he felt distant and out of place, as though there were a wall between them and him. He also said, with a flat certainty, that people could not be trusted. That belief showed up in small but concrete ways: he held back from relying on others, avoided sharing what was happening with him, and kept conversations guarded. He said that once someone had seen enough of him, they might leave, misunderstand him, or fail him when it mattered. That mistrust had made him quieter and more withdrawn, even though part of him still wanted connection.

Photography had once felt like a way for Minh to notice the world carefully, but now his work environment also brought the war experience too close at times. He worked around sudden flashes, mechanical clicks, and abrupt noises from equipment or traffic when shooting on location, and those ordinary sounds could catch him off guard and make him tense or jump. He found himself watching the space around him more than the scene in front of him, scanning for anything that might suddenly change. He had begun avoiding some assignments and situations that made him feel exposed, and that avoidance had started to affect his routine and his relationships with clients and friends who did not understand why he sometimes pulled back at the last minute. By the time he sought help, Minh was exhausted by the constant state of alertness, the vivid intrusions, and the weight of believing he had failed the people he was supposed to protect. What finally brought him in was the growing fear that he would keep living as if the attack were happening all over again, and his hope, however guarded, was that treatment might help him feel that he belonged somewhere again without needing to stay on guard every second.
